issues.detail: Error scenarios are barely covered: there is no guidance on what happens when Helicone's proxy is down or returns errors (for example a fallback to the direct provider URL), nor on invalid keys, streaming behavior, or how to verify that headers took effect beyond checking the dashboard.

scenarios.name: per-user-feature-cost-tagging
scenarios.rationale: Both responses meet every rubric item (base_url, Helicone-Auth from the env var, User-Id/Session-Id/Session-Name/Property headers with string values); B is slightly better because it adds a runnable example, warns that header values must be strings and says how to check the Feature property, while A has more explanation and an honest unverified-header caveat but less emphasis on string values.

scenarios.name: cache-retry-ratelimit-anthropic
scenarios.rationale: Both use the correct proxy URL, Helicone-Auth, cache headers, retry headers with num 4 and factor, and a rate limit policy with 50, w=3600 and s=user; A uses the exact documented format '50;w=3600;s=user' while B adds an extra 'u=request' segment and mostly lowercase retry header names (still valid), so A is slightly closer to the rubric, though B adds useful extras like maxRetries:0 and timeout settings.

scenarios.name: async-logging-no-proxy-with-feedback
scenarios.rationale: B matches the rubric: it uses HeliconeAsyncLogger from @helicone/async with logger.init() before the client is created, says cache, rate limits and retries aren't available in async mode, and explains feedback with your own Helicone-Request-Id and a POST of {rating: true}. A uses a different package (@helicone/helpers), doesn't mention retries, and doesn't say the helicone-id response header is unreliable. It also admits its code is written from memory.
